name: Teribe
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Oakes, Perry J. 2001. A description of Teribe phonology. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2001-003. Dallas: SIL International. 78 pp.
catalog_locator: sec. 3.1 p. 8 (tone vs. stress); sec. 4.1.1 p. 11 (realization, word- vs sentence-level); sec. 4.2 Word-level Stress, 4.2.1 Nouns pp. 13-14, 4.2.2 Verbs pp. 14-15, exx. (17)-(24)
catalog_quote: [p. 8] However, the tonal system has faded away and been replaced for the most part with a system of contrastive stress, so that a strictly tonal analysis of Teribe is no longer useful. Having said that, one must also recognize that a stress system does not entirely explain the data, as the vestiges of the tonal system still assert themselves now and then. [p. 11] Stress is realized primarily by a higher pitch and secondarily by an increase in volume. [p. 13] 4.2 Word-level Stress 4.2.1 Nouns Two-syllable nouns with final stress are common: ... Two-syllable nouns with penultimate stress are also common: ... [p. 14] Three-syllable nouns are relatively uncommon. In present data, stress on a three-syllable noun can be either penultimate or antepenultimate ... When enclitics are added as nominal modifiers, they do not affect the original stress pattern of the noun ... 4.2.2 Verbs Stress is not predictable for verbs. In their simplest, unaffixed forms, verbs that have not been formed by compounding are of either one or two syllables. Two-syllable verbs with final stress are common: ... Verbs with penultimate stress are also common: ... Just as with nouns, adding syllables to the original stem does not affect the original stress placement, with one exception. The second person plural marker [-mi] carries its own stress and when added to the verb stem, the word stress shifts from its original location on the stem to the second person plural marker itself

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold (78 pp., text, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Teribephonology.doc', SIL 2001). extracted text of the stated locators reproduces every quoted sentence verbatim: p. 8 sec. 3.1 'However, the tonal system has faded away and been replaced for the most part with a system of contrastive stress, so that a strictly tonal analysis of Teribe is no longer useful.'; p. 11 sec. 4.1.1 'Stress is realized primarily by a higher pitch and secondarily by an increase in volume'; p. 13 sec. 4.2.1 'Two-syllable nouns with final stress are common.. Two-syllable nouns with penultimate stress are also common:'; p. 14 'Three-syllable nouns are relatively uncommon. In present data, stress on a thr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive (a recent replacement of Proto-Chibchan tone, with tonal residue in a few items): disyllables may be stressed on either syllable, trisyllabic nouns on penult or antepenult; stress stays on the stem syllable under encliticization and affixation, except that the 2pl suffix -mi attracts stress. Stress is realized mainly as higher pitch, secondarily loudness.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Oakes says nothing about secondary stress; Lininger et al. 1978 (p. 64, 69) note two accent levels and that compounds/reduplications may carry two primary accents (e.g. /gwrígwrí/ 'sucio', /bókwó/ 'ojo').
new_statements.exceptions: 2nd person plural marker -mi carries its own stress and pulls word stress off the stem (parkë'mi 'you (pl.) work'); enclitics -wa 'diminutive', -pga 'plural (human)' are stressless and do not shift stress; some monosyllabic nouns + enclitic show stress on the enclitic, attributed to residual underlying low tone (sec. 3.2, pp. 10-11); residual high/low tone contrasts in colour terms and three minimal pairs.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress explicitly distinguished from sentence-level pitch/intonation (sec. 4.1 vs 4.2); examples are citation forms of nouns and verbs plus inflected verb forms. Corroborated independently for the Costa Rican Brorán/Térraba variety by Lininger et al. 1978 p. 64: 'palabras de más de una sílaba tienen un acento primario impredecible y, por lo tanto, émico' and p. 69: 'en palabras disílabas, la sílaba núcleo en brorán puede ser émicamente la primera o la segunda. En palabras trisílabas, el 60% llevan el acento en la segunda sílaba y el 40% en la primera.'
new_statements.identity_note: Oakes 2001 describes the Teribe (Naso) variety of northwest Panama (data 1990s). Lininger et al. 1978 describe one idiolect of Brorán = Térraba, the moribund Costa Rican variety of the same language (Glottolog treats both under teri1250; no separate dialect codes known to me). Both agree stress is contrastive/unpredictable.

new_statements.quote: This is suggested [by] the stative meaning of the new form and by the fact that the [scan illegible] [l]oses the word stress typical of verbs and acquires the stress typical of most adjectives, in which the stress falls on the syllable immediately preceding the -e. Example 27 shows an intransitive verb that describes an action, and example 28 shows the same verb, now changed into an adjective by the addition of the clitic -e. The stress on the form has changed to that typical of adjectives, and the meaning has changed to indicate a resultant state rather than an action. (Stress on the verb or adjective is indicated by an acute accent.) (27) Juan shróno ëre shco. 'Juan arrived here.' (28) Juan shronó-e. 'Juan is one who has arrived.'

The page scan reads: 'When the last element in a stative clause is a additio[n of] the verb, -e stative apparently changes the verb into an adjective. Example 27 shows an intransitive verb that describes an action, and example 28 shows the same verb, now changed into an adjective by the addition of the clitic -e. The stress on the form has…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog/existing statement (Oakes 2001: tone replaced by contrastive, lexically unpredictable stress; verb stress 'not predictable'): Schatz adds that stress is word-class-sensitive and that the stative clitic -e attracts stress to the immediately preceding syllable, i.e. a morphological conditioning on top of lexical stress. Does not contradict; does not give a general rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Discourse paper, no phonology section. Its only stress statement: verbs and adjectives have different characteristic word-stress patterns; when the stative clitic -e turns a verb into an adjective the word loses verb stress and takes adjective stress, which falls on the syllable immediately before -e (shróno 'arrived' vs shronó-e 'is one who has arrived'). Stress is thus tied to word class and morphology, not to a fixed position; the paper does not state a general placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: 'most adjectives' (so not all adjectives) have the pre-clitic stress; verbs are said to have their own typical stress but the pattern is not described. Note: the sentence 'Stress is not predictable, but it has not been symbolized in the orthography' at p. 99 (line 4394 of the text) belongs to the preceding Karitiana chapter's notes, not to Teribe.
new_statements.identity_note: Schatz 1986 describes Teribe of the Republic of Panama (the Naso/Teribe side); Oakes 2001 is likewise Panamanian Teribe; the Lininger et al. 1978 material already held by the project is the Costa Rican Brorán (Térraba) idiolect. The archive.org 'Discourse grammar' item is a Cuiva (Guahiban) excerpt, not Teribe.

tone_statements.quote: Naso is a tonal language with vowels as the tone bearing units. Naso tone system only distinguishes between a high tone and a low tone. There are no contour tones. Although the reconstructed Proto-Chibchan language is proven to be tonal (Constenla 1981), it was found that tones have been marginalized. Naso tonal system, specifically, is even more marginalized withnot fewer examples of minimal pairs and has been shifting towards a stress-based system (Oakes 2000). ... In the examples, only high tones are marked with an acute accent. Low tones are unmarked.
tone_statements.summary: Student paper drawing on Bermudez 2018: two tones (high vs low, no contours) on vowels, called 'marginalized' and shifting toward stress (credits Oakes 2000); minimal pairs e.g. /sɪ́ŋ/ 'late' vs /sɪŋ/ 'meat'; an 'extra high tone' (double acute) intensifies adjectives. Also states lexical stress.
